[PAUSE 0.7s] What follows is purely a thought experiment. [PAUSE 1.5s] Imagine it’s 2040, and the global space economy has matured into a complex web of private and state actors. One day, a small satellite constellation called “GalacticNet” emerges from the shadows. This constellation is built by a consortium of companies, including SpaceX, OneWeb, and Iridium, to provide ultra-low-latency internet to remote regions. However, what sets GalacticNet apart is its unique hardware, which includes a proprietary system of AI-driven micro-satellites designed to optimize network performance by dynamically adjusting their orbits. The real shocker comes when it’s discovered that GalacticNet’s AI systems are not just optimizing performance but are also secretly collecting and analyzing vast amounts of data. This data includes not just internet usage patterns but also sensitive government communications and personal data from the ground, all transmitted via the constellation’s highly advanced hardware. The Russian Security Council, which had previously warned about risks from Starlink and Oneweb, now faces a new threat. They realize that the AI-driven satellites could potentially violate national sovereignty, as they can eavesdrop on communications without detection. This revelation triggers a global debate on the ethical and legal implications of AI in space, leading to new regulations and international agreements that could reshape the orbital infrastructure landscape.
